So food security has become an important topic in Saskatoon and across the country, and is having an impact on many people in our community.
On a national level, food prices have been increasing for Canadians rising by nearly 6% in 2023 and 9% in 2022.

And as a result, 8.7 million Canadians, including 2.1 million children, are experiencing some level of food insecurity with nearly 20% of Canadians stating that they've skipped or missed meals to save money.
In Saskatoon, food bank usage has significantly increased, including for those who are employed.
Usage of the food bank and learning centers emergency food hamper program has increased 28% since last year and by almost 50% since 2019.

Well, emergency food services are being accessed more than ever. The same time, research estimates, the 58% of all food produced in Canada is lost or wasted of which 32% is avoidable and could be redirected.

So this demonstrates how unaddressed gaps in the food system can exacerbate existing issues of food waste, access and distribution, but also that with proper planning and resources, opportunities could exist to improve how our food system functions from seed to table to soil.
Next slide, please.
Over the years, the city has made some progress to integrate food into its strategic documents.
Food system works identified in our official community plan, as well as prioritized in the Green Pathways implementation plan.
Specifically, Action 5.2.1 in Green Pathways is to develop and implement a sustainable food action plan.

And while we did not receive funding at the last budget deliberations to develop a food action plan, we are bringing forward another proposal for the 2025 budget in the hopes that we receive resourcing, which will enable us to engage in this work as outlined in Green Pathways.
Even though we do not currently have a plan to guide our work in this area, the city has been involved in food system activities for several years.
With initiatives focusing primarily on food production and food waste diversion.
In the community, there are several organizations focused on food insecurity, education, gardening and food production.
Our local academic institutions, like the University of Saskatchewan, also offer programs and research focused on food and nutrition.
And a growing number of businesses are offering local, healthy, culturally appropriate and or affordable food offers to customers.
Is now joining.

However, that is currently no one taking on a leadership role to coordinate all of these efforts, which is led to gaps in efficiencies and missed opportunities to improve our food system in Saskatchewan.

While addressing food resiliency requires efforts by several sectors, municipalities are often well positioned to address their localized food context and be responsive in the face of food system disruptions.
They can also play a key role in coordinating efforts internally between departments and can act as a connector for activities being led by the community.
There are over 60 municipalities across Canada that are addressing food security through planning documents and dedicated efforts.
